title: Early player influences: Goodman, Bigard, Trumbauer, Teagarden, Miff Mole
summary: From Red Nichols records and Ellington he heard Benny Goodman, Barney Bigard, Frank Trumbauer and Jack Teagarden, whose assurance impressed him; he was not impressed by Miff Mole.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: All right. Some of the people you were interested in as players at the time.
Well, from those early records, particularly with the Red Nichols sides, I got to hear people like Benny Goodman for the first time.
And even earlier sessions, I heard

people -- oh, what's the clarinetist? Earlier than Peewee Russell and people like that. This was a Chicago clarinetist and he played very well, and he impressed me. I just can't think of the name for the moment.

MR. HERMAN: But I think also the fact that I was hearing these growling sounds from the Ellington group and uses of plungers with the trumpets and trombones and -- this all impressed me very much, along with the early Barney Bigard. And I wasn't -- and Frank Trumbauer was naturally a big influence. I think he had to be a big influence on some other people, because he was the first one to use the glissando as a means of making his feelings known, and I think Johnny Hodges would have to feel pretty much the same way as I did.

I first heard -- and it's an amazing thing, but when you're very young, a difference in age of a matter of four or five years is a big difference. And as you grow older, it becomes less and less important. But I do remember hearing Jack Teagarden for the first time. It was on one of the Red Nichols records. And I never could get -- I never could get over the fact that I -- it just gave me the feeling that this man had never made a mistake in his whole life, and didn't plan on making any, musically speaking.

And this gives a person -- I realized then what a great feeling of relaxation and assurance it gives your audience, if you're that kind of player. Because not so many were. And I felt a great deal of admiration and respect for him. For that reason, and many others, of course.

But these were some of the earliest sounds that I do remember, and just as I thought he was so fantastic, I was not impressed, for instance, by Miff Mole. I couldn't find anything happening. And yet, he was very fluent and a very together trombone player for those times and days. And, of course, to me Benny Goodman as time went on proved that he was a genius at keeping the instrumental sound of an instrument where it should be and being able to convey his thoughts and ideas as he did.
